name: Finance for Technology and Business Leaders
description: Budgets and forecasting, financial statements, margins, subscription unit economics, pricing, capex and opex, build and run cost, FinOps, vendor contracts, investment appraisal, headcount and project costing, working capital, controls and tax awareness, fundraising and board reporting for leaders who own budgets and decisions.

groups.vendor: vendor contract term or negotiation concept

cards.subject: The annual budget
says: sets planned revenue and spending for the coming financial year
gives each budget owner a spending envelope to manage against
is the baseline that actual results are later compared with
cards.use: need a fixed yardstick to judge results against at year end
not: is updated every month to reflect the latest outlook

cards.subject: A rolling forecast
says: is re-projected every period so it always looks a fixed number of periods ahead
replaces a fixed year-end horizon with a moving one
lets leaders react to new information without waiting for the next budget cycle
cards.use: need the outlook to stay current as conditions change
not: is frozen once the board approves it

cards.subject: Zero-based budgeting
says: requires every cost line to be justified from nothing each cycle
does not treat last year's spend as the starting point
exposes legacy spending that nobody can defend
cards.use: suspect that old costs persist only out of habit
not: adds a fixed percentage to last year's figures

cards.subject: Incremental budgeting
says: starts from last period's figures and adjusts them up or down
is quick to prepare but can carry old waste forward
assumes the existing cost base is broadly right
cards.use: need a fast, low-effort budget round
not: justifies every cost line from scratch

cards.subject: Variance analysis
says: compares actual results with the budget or forecast and explains the gap
labels a gap favourable or unfavourable depending on its effect on profit
looks for causes such as price, volume or timing
cards.use: see actual spend differ from plan and must explain why
not: predicts next year's revenue from market trends

cards.subject: A driver-based forecast
says: builds revenue and cost from operational drivers such as headcount, customers or usage
changes automatically when a driver assumption is changed
links the finance model to what the business actually does
cards.use: want the forecast to move when sales volume or hiring plans change
not: extrapolates last year's totals by a flat percentage

cards.subject: Bottom-up budgeting
says: builds the budget from detailed estimates supplied by each team
tends to give accurate detail but can inflate the total
needs consolidation and challenge before it fits the company target
cards.use: need owners to commit to figures they helped build
not: starts from a company-wide target handed down from leadership

cards.subject: Top-down budgeting
says: starts from a company-level target and allocates it to departments
reflects strategic priorities but may ignore operational detail
is quick but can feel imposed on the teams
cards.use: must fit spending to a fixed funding envelope
not: asks each team to estimate its own costs first

cards.subject: Scenario planning
says: models several possible futures such as base, upside and downside
shows which assumptions the plan is most sensitive to
prepares triggers for action before a scenario occurs
cards.use: face uncertain demand and want to pre-agree responses
not: picks a single most likely forecast and ignores alternatives

cards.subject: A contingency reserve
says: holds budget back for risks that are expected but not yet specific
is released only under a defined approval
prevents every small overrun from becoming a budget change request
cards.use: expect some unplanned cost but cannot name it yet
not: is extra money spread into every team's normal spending

cards.subject: The income statement
says: reports revenue, costs and profit over a period of time
is also called the profit and loss account or P&L
ends with net income as the bottom line
cards.use: need to know whether the business made a profit last quarter
not: lists what the company owns and owes on one date

cards.subject: The balance sheet
says: shows assets, liabilities and equity at a single point in time
must balance so that assets equal liabilities plus equity
shows what the company owns and what it owes
cards.use: need to see the financial position on the last day of the month
not: reports revenue and costs across a period

cards.subject: The cash flow statement
says: reports cash moving in and out across operating, investing and financing activities
reconciles profit to the change in the cash balance
explains why cash and profit differ
cards.use: see profit rise but the bank balance fall
not: measures profit using accruals only

cards.subject: Accrual accounting
says: records revenue when earned and costs when incurred
matches costs to the period in which they help earn revenue
can show a profit before any cash has been received
cards.use: need results to reflect work done rather than payments made
not: records an item only when cash changes hands

cards.subject: Cash-basis accounting
says: records income and expense only when cash is received or paid
is simple but can distort results across periods
is mostly used by very small businesses
cards.use: want the simplest record of money in and out
not: recognises revenue as soon as a contract is signed

cards.subject: Revenue recognition
says: decides when and how much revenue can be recorded as earned
spreads subscription revenue across the service period
depends on delivery of the promised service rather than on invoicing
cards.use: sell an annual subscription and must book it correctly
not: records the full contract value as revenue on the invoice date

cards.subject: Deferred revenue
says: is cash received for service not yet delivered
sits on the balance sheet as a liability
turns into revenue as the service is delivered
cards.use: get paid for the full year up front
not: counts immediately as profit for the period

cards.subject: EBITDA
says: is earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation
is used to compare operating performance without financing and accounting effects
ignores the cost of capital spending
cards.use: want a view of operating profit before financing and non-cash charges
not: equals the cash generated by the business

cards.subject: Net income
says: is revenue minus all expenses including interest and tax
is the bottom line of the income statement
is the amount that flows into retained earnings if not paid out
cards.use: need the profit remaining after every cost
not: excludes tax and interest

cards.subject: Accounts receivable
says: are amounts customers owe for work already invoiced
are an asset on the balance sheet
turn into cash when the customer pays
cards.use: have invoiced a client who has not paid yet
not: are amounts the company owes to suppliers

cards.subject: Accounts payable
says: are amounts the company owes suppliers for goods or services received
are a liability on the balance sheet
delay cash leaving the business until the bill is paid
cards.use: have received a supplier invoice that is not yet paid
not: are amounts customers owe the company

cards.subject: Gross margin
says: is revenue minus the direct cost of delivering the product or service, as a share of revenue
shows how much of each unit of revenue remains to cover overhead
is calculated before operating expenses
cards.use: want to know how profitable delivery itself is
not: subtracts all overheads and tax

cards.subject: Contribution margin
says: is revenue minus variable costs
shows what each sale adds towards fixed costs and profit
is used to find the break-even point
cards.use: decide whether one more unit or customer is worth serving
not: includes fixed overheads in the cost

cards.subject: Operating margin
says: is operating profit as a share of revenue
includes operating expenses such as sales, marketing and admin
is measured before interest and tax
cards.use: want to see profitability after running costs but before financing
not: stops at direct delivery costs

cards.subject: Cost of goods sold
says: is the direct cost of producing what was sold in the period
for software businesses is often called cost of revenue and includes hosting and support
is subtracted from revenue to give gross profit
cards.use: need to separate delivery cost from overhead
not: includes the marketing budget

cards.subject: The break-even point
says: is the volume at which total revenue equals total cost
is fixed costs divided by contribution margin per unit
shows how many sales are needed before profit begins
cards.use: need to know how much must be sold to cover fixed costs
not: is the point at which cash is fully paid back by investors

cards.subject: A fixed cost
says: stays the same in total when volume changes within a normal range
includes items such as rent and salaried staff
has to be covered whether or not anything is sold
cards.use: are costing an item that does not rise with each sale
not: rises in direct proportion to units sold

cards.subject: A variable cost
says: changes in proportion to the volume produced or sold
includes items such as payment fees and per-unit hosting
is subtracted from price to get contribution margin
cards.use: are costing an item that rises with each sale
not: is the same whatever the volume

cards.subject: Markup
says: is the amount added to cost, expressed as a percentage of cost
is always larger than the margin on the same sale
is the figure used when setting prices as cost plus an addition
cards.use: price from cost and must not confuse the percentage with margin
not: is expressed as a percentage of the selling price

cards.subject: Operating leverage
says: describes how a high share of fixed costs magnifies profit swings as volume changes
means profit grows faster than revenue once fixed costs are covered
also means profit falls faster than revenue when volume drops
cards.use: want to judge how risky a fixed-cost-heavy model is in a downturn
not: means variable costs are the largest part of the cost base

cards.subject: MRR
says: is the predictable subscription revenue normalised to a month
excludes one-off fees such as setup charges
is the building block that multiplies by twelve to give ARR
cards.use: track monthly recurring subscription income
not: includes one-off consulting fees

cards.subject: ARR
says: is the annualised value of recurring subscription revenue
excludes one-off and non-recurring fees
is monthly recurring revenue multiplied by twelve
cards.use: need one headline figure for the yearly recurring revenue base
not: is the total cash collected in the year

cards.subject: CAC
says: is the cost of sales and marketing needed to win one new customer
is total acquisition spend divided by new customers won
is compared with customer value to judge growth efficiency
cards.use: want to know what it costs to win one customer
not: is the revenue a customer brings over their lifetime

cards.subject: LTV
says: estimates the gross profit a customer generates over their relationship
is commonly approximated as margin-adjusted revenue per period divided by churn rate
should use margin rather than revenue to be meaningful
cards.use: want to know how much a customer is worth before deciding how much to spend winning one
not: is the cost of acquiring the customer

cards.subject: CAC payback
says: is the time for a customer's gross profit to recover the cost of acquiring them
is CAC divided by monthly gross profit per customer
is shorter when acquisition is efficient
cards.use: need to know how quickly acquisition spend returns as cash
not: is the time until the contract renews

cards.subject: Logo churn
says: is the percentage of customers lost in a period
counts each customer equally regardless of size
is customers lost divided by customers at the start
cards.use: want to know how many customers leave regardless of their spend
not: measures lost revenue weighted by contract value

cards.subject: Revenue churn
says: is the percentage of recurring revenue lost to cancellations and downgrades
weights each customer by what they pay
can be high even when few customers leave
cards.use: fear that your biggest accounts are leaving
not: counts every customer equally

cards.subject: Net revenue retention
says: measures revenue from existing customers after expansion, contraction and churn
exceeds 100 percent when expansion outweighs losses
excludes revenue from new customers
cards.use: want to know whether the existing base grows by itself
not: includes new logos won in the period

cards.subject: Gross revenue retention
says: measures revenue kept from existing customers after churn and contraction only
cannot exceed 100 percent
ignores expansion revenue
cards.use: want to see how leaky the base is without upsell hiding it
not: can rise above 100 percent through upsell

cards.subject: The LTV to CAC ratio
says: compares the lifetime value of a customer with the cost of winning them
signals unprofitable growth when it is low
signals possible under-investment in growth when it is very high
cards.use: need a single ratio for acquisition efficiency
not: measures how fast the cost is repaid

cards.subject: Expansion revenue
says: is extra recurring revenue from existing customers through upsell or cross-sell
feeds net revenue retention
is cheaper to win than a new customer in many models
cards.use: sell more seats or modules to current customers
not: is revenue from first-time customers

cards.subject: Per-seat pricing
says: charges according to the number of named or active users
scales revenue with customer headcount
can discourage adoption if customers limit users to save cost
cards.use: sell a tool whose value grows with each user
not: charges for the amount consumed

cards.subject: Usage-based pricing
says: charges according to consumption such as calls, storage or transactions
ties revenue to the value or load the customer creates
makes revenue and bills less predictable
cards.use: sell something where cost to serve rises with use
not: charges one fixed fee regardless of use

cards.subject: Tiered pricing
says: offers several packages at different prices and feature levels
lets customers self-select by need and budget
relies on clear differences between tiers
cards.use: serve customers of very different sizes
not: offers a single package at a single price

cards.subject: Cost-plus pricing
says: sets price by adding a margin to the cost
guarantees a margin if costs are estimated correctly
ignores what the customer values the output at
cards.use: price from known cost with no market reference
not: sets price by the benefit the customer receives

cards.subject: Value-based pricing
says: sets price by the benefit the customer receives
can earn more than cost-plus when the value is high
requires understanding the customer's economics
cards.use: deliver a result worth far more to the customer than it costs to produce
not: sets price by adding a margin to cost

cards.subject: Time-and-materials pricing
says: bills actual hours worked at agreed rates plus expenses
places the budget risk mostly on the client
suits work whose scope cannot be fixed in advance
cards.use: cannot define the scope well enough to quote a fixed price
not: fixes the total fee before work starts

cards.subject: Fixed-price pricing
says: agrees a total fee for a defined scope before work starts
places overrun risk on the supplier
relies on clear scope and change control
cards.use: have a well-defined scope and the client wants cost certainty
not: bills for every hour worked regardless of the quote

cards.subject: A retainer
says: is a recurring fee for reserved capacity or ongoing availability
gives the supplier predictable income
can lose value for the client if the capacity goes unused
cards.use: need predictable monthly income from a long-term client
not: bills only for completed deliverables

cards.subject: Outcome-based pricing
says: links the fee to a measured result achieved for the customer
shares performance risk between supplier and customer
needs an agreed and attributable measure of success
cards.use: are confident of delivering a measurable result and want to be paid for it
not: charges for hours regardless of result

cards.subject: Capex
says: is spending on assets that provide benefit over several periods
is recorded on the balance sheet and spread over time
is the category for spending that creates or extends a long-lived asset
cards.use: buy something that will serve the business for years
not: is fully charged to the income statement in the year of purchase

cards.subject: Opex
says: is spending on the day-to-day running of the business
is charged to the income statement in the period it occurs
includes items such as salaries and subscriptions
cards.use: pay a cost that is consumed within the period
not: is spread over the useful life of an asset

cards.subject: Capitalised software development
says: records qualifying development cost as an asset rather than an expense
generally applies once a project is viable and the company intends to complete it
excludes maintenance and research-phase work in most frameworks
cards.use: build software that will bring benefit over several years
not: treats every engineer's salary as an asset

cards.subject: Depreciation
says: spreads the cost of a tangible asset over its useful life
reduces profit without any cash leaving
applies to equipment rather than intangible assets
cards.use: own equipment that wears out over several years
not: is a cash payment to the supplier

cards.subject: Amortisation
says: spreads the cost of an intangible asset over its useful life
applies to items such as capitalised software and licences
reduces profit without any cash leaving
cards.use: hold a capitalised software asset that will be used for several years
not: applies only to physical equipment

cards.subject: Impairment
says: writes an asset down when its value falls below its recorded amount
is recognised as a charge to profit
is triggered by events such as abandoning a product
cards.use: cancel a project whose capitalised cost can no longer be recovered
not: is the normal scheduled spreading of cost

cards.subject: Build cost
says: is the one-off cost of creating a system or product
includes design, development and testing effort
is only part of the total cost of owning a system
cards.use: are quoting what it takes to deliver the first release
not: is the recurring cost of operating the system

cards.subject: Run cost
says: is the recurring cost of operating and supporting a system once live
includes hosting, licences, support and maintenance
often exceeds the build cost over a long life
cards.use: have launched and must budget to keep the service going
not: is the one-off cost of creating the system

cards.subject: Total cost of ownership
says: adds acquisition, operation, support and exit costs over the whole life
exposes costs that a purchase price alone hides
is used to compare options fairly
cards.use: compare two options with different up-front and running costs
not: is the up-front purchase price only

cards.subject: Opportunity cost
says: is the value of the next best alternative given up
does not appear as a line in the accounts
applies to scarce resources such as engineering time
cards.use: commit a team to one project and must name what is forgone
not: is the cash paid for the chosen option

cards.subject: A sunk cost
says: is money already spent that cannot be recovered
should not drive a decision about future spending
is often wrongly used to justify continuing a failing project
cards.use: hesitate to stop a project because so much has been spent
not: is a future cost that can still be avoided

cards.subject: Marginal cost
says: is the extra cost of producing one more unit
is low for software with little extra cost per customer
guides pricing floors for additional volume
cards.use: decide whether to accept one more order at a lower price
not: is the average cost across all units

cards.subject: Cost of delay
says: is the value lost for each period a deliverable is late
helps prioritise by comparing delay costs of competing work
turns urgency into a number
cards.use: must decide which of two projects to start first
not: is the budget overrun on a late project

cards.subject: Technical debt interest
says: is the extra ongoing cost caused by shortcuts left in the system
shows up as slower delivery and more incidents
grows if the underlying shortcut is not repaid
cards.use: must explain to finance why slow delivery has a financial cost
not: is the interest on a bank loan used to buy software

cards.subject: FinOps
says: is the practice of bringing financial accountability to cloud spending
brings engineering, finance and business teams together on cost
aims to improve value from cloud rather than to cut spending blindly
cards.use: want engineering and finance to share responsibility for cloud cost
not: is a tool that automatically buys cheaper servers

cards.subject: Showback
says: reports to teams what their usage costs without billing them
builds cost awareness without moving money
relies on accurate cost allocation
cards.use: want teams to see their spend before any internal charging
not: transfers the cost to the team's budget

cards.subject: Chargeback
says: bills each team's budget for the cloud cost they incur
makes teams financially accountable for their use
needs trustworthy allocation or it causes disputes
cards.use: want cloud cost to land in the budget of the team that incurred it
not: only reports cost for information

cards.subject: Cost allocation tags
says: are labels on resources that attribute their cost to a team or product
fail to attribute spend when resources are left untagged
make showback and chargeback possible
cards.use: cannot tell which team caused a growing bill
not: compress data to reduce storage fees

cards.subject: Rightsizing
says: matches resource size to the actual workload
reduces waste from over-provisioned capacity
is usually done before buying a commitment
cards.use: find servers running far below capacity
not: buys a long-term discount on current capacity

cards.subject: A commitment discount
says: offers a lower rate in exchange for committing to a level of usage over a term
wastes money if the committed usage is not used
suits steady, predictable workloads
cards.use: have a stable baseline of usage that will last
not: gives a discount for interruptible spare capacity

cards.subject: Spot capacity
says: offers spare capacity at a lower price that the provider can reclaim
suits fault-tolerant or interruptible workloads
is unsuitable for work that cannot tolerate sudden loss
cards.use: run batch jobs that can restart safely
not: guarantees capacity for a fixed term

cards.subject: Cloud unit economics
says: relates cloud cost to a business measure such as cost per order or per customer
shows whether cost grows faster than the business
separates healthy growth from waste
cards.use: see the bill grow and need to know whether that is fine
not: tracks the total bill without any business measure

cards.subject: Cost anomaly detection
says: alerts on unexpected spikes in spend
helps catch misconfiguration or runaway workloads early
complements budgets by watching patterns not totals
cards.use: want to hear about a spend spike within days, not at month end
not: allocates shared cost to teams

cards.subject: Data egress charges
says: are fees for moving data out of a cloud provider or across regions
can make architecture choices or migrations costly
are easy to overlook when designing data-heavy systems
cards.use: plan a design that moves large volumes of data between regions
not: are fees for storing data at rest

cards.subject: Shared cost allocation
says: splits the cost of shared platform items among the teams that benefit
needs an agreed fair basis such as usage or headcount
avoids leaving untagged shared spend with nobody
cards.use: must charge teams for a shared cluster or network
not: attributes each cost to one team through tags

cards.subject: A master services agreement
says: sets the general terms that govern all later work orders with a supplier
lets individual projects be agreed quickly under standing terms
separates long-lived legal terms from project-specific scope
cards.use: expect to buy several pieces of work from the same supplier
not: fixes the price and scope of one single project

cards.subject: A statement of work
says: defines the scope, deliverables, timeline and price of a specific piece of work
sits under a master agreement
is where acceptance criteria are normally written down
cards.use: need to define exactly what a supplier will deliver this time
not: sets the general legal terms for the whole relationship

cards.subject: A service level agreement
says: states measurable service commitments such as availability or response time
usually pairs commitments with remedies when they are missed
is only useful if the measure is clearly defined
cards.use: depend on a supplier and need a measurable promise
not: describes the commercial price of the service

cards.subject: A service credit
says: is a remedy that reduces future charges when an SLA is missed
is often the main financial remedy a supplier offers
rarely covers the real business loss from an outage
cards.use: want to know what you receive when a supplier misses its uptime promise
not: is a payment covering all losses from the outage

cards.subject: An auto-renewal clause
says: renews the contract automatically unless notice is given within a window
can lock in another term if the deadline is missed
makes the notice date an important diary item
cards.use: hold a contract that continues unless someone acts before a date
not: ends the contract automatically on the expiry date

cards.subject: Termination for convenience
says: allows one party to end the contract without proving a breach
usually requires notice and may involve a fee
gives flexibility that fixed-term contracts lack
cards.use: want to leave the contract early without the supplier having failed
not: allows exit only after a material breach

cards.subject: A price escalator
says: sets how the price rises over the contract term
may be fixed, or linked to an index
should be capped so future cost is predictable
cards.use: sign a multi-year contract and fear later price increases
not: is a discount that grows with volume

cards.subject: A minimum commitment
says: obliges the customer to pay for a set volume or spend even if it is not used
trades flexibility for a lower unit price
creates risk when demand falls below the commitment
cards.use: are offered a lower rate for guaranteeing spend
not: lets you pay only for what is consumed

cards.subject: A volume discount
says: reduces the unit price as quantity or spend increases
is earned by consumption rather than promised in advance
rewards scale
cards.use: expect to buy increasingly large quantities
not: requires a fixed prepaid commitment

cards.subject: A data portability clause
says: secures the customer's right to retrieve their data in a usable format
reduces lock-in when leaving a supplier
should state format and timeframe
cards.use: worry about getting data back if you leave the supplier
not: extends the supplier's right to keep the data

cards.subject: An indemnification clause
says: makes one party compensate the other for specified third-party claims or losses
allocates risk for matters such as intellectual property infringement
is a risk-allocation term to be reviewed by legal counsel
cards.use: want to know who bears the cost if a third party sues over the supplier's product
not: lets either party leave without penalty

cards.subject: BATNA
says: is the best alternative to a negotiated agreement
sets the walk-away point in a negotiation
is strengthened by having credible other suppliers
cards.use: enter a negotiation and need to know your fallback if talks fail
not: is the opening price the supplier proposes

cards.subject: Return on investment
says: is the gain from an investment minus its cost, divided by its cost
is expressed as a percentage
ignores the timing of the cash flows
cards.use: want a quick measure of how much an investment returns relative to cost
not: discounts future cash flows to present value

cards.subject: The payback period
says: is the time taken for cumulative cash inflows to recover the initial investment
ignores cash flows after recovery
favours quick returns
cards.use: need to know how soon the money is recovered
not: measures total value created over the whole life

cards.subject: Net present value
says: is the sum of future cash flows discounted to today minus the initial outlay
approves an investment only when it is positive at the chosen discount rate
is stated as a currency amount rather than a percentage
cards.use: must compare investments with different timing of cash flows
not: ignores when cash arrives

cards.subject: Internal rate of return
says: is the discount rate at which an investment's net present value is zero
is compared with the hurdle rate to accept or reject
can mislead when cash flows change sign several times
cards.use: want a single percentage return that includes timing
not: is the cost of the loan funding the project

cards.subject: The time value of money
says: is the principle that money today is worth more than the same amount later
is the reason future cash flows are discounted
reflects the chance to earn a return and the risk of waiting
cards.use: must explain why delayed benefits are worth less
not: says inflation is always zero

cards.subject: The discount rate
says: converts future cash flows into present value
rises to reflect greater risk or cost of capital
lowers the present value of distant cash flows when it increases
cards.use: must pick the rate used to value future benefits
not: is the price reduction offered to a customer

cards.subject: The hurdle rate
says: is the minimum return a project must achieve to be approved
is usually based on the cost of capital plus a risk allowance
is the benchmark an internal rate of return is compared with
cards.use: must set the bar a proposed project has to clear
not: is the highest return the company has ever earned

cards.subject: The discounted payback period
says: is the time to recover the investment using discounted cash flows
is longer than the simple payback period for the same project
recovers the investment only after each period's cash flow has been discounted
cards.use: want a payback test that respects the time value of money
not: ignores the discount rate

cards.subject: Sensitivity analysis
says: changes one assumption at a time to see its effect on the result
shows which assumptions the answer depends on most
helps focus validation effort on the shaky inputs
cards.use: doubt the assumptions behind a business case
not: models several full scenarios at once

cards.subject: A business case
says: sets out costs, benefits, risks and options to justify a decision
compares doing something with doing nothing
should state its assumptions so they can be challenged
cards.use: must persuade leadership to approve funding
not: is a record of completed project spending

cards.subject: Fully loaded cost
says: is the full cost of an employee including salary, benefits, taxes and overhead
is higher than salary alone
is the correct basis for project costing
cards.use: need the true cost of a team member to price work
not: is the salary printed on the contract

cards.subject: Utilisation rate
says: is billable hours as a share of available hours
measures how much of capacity earns revenue
can be pushed so high that there is no time for training or sales
cards.use: want to know how much of a team's time is billed
not: is revenue divided by headcount

cards.subject: Realisation rate
says: compares revenue actually billed with the revenue at standard rates for the time worked
drops when time is written off or discounted
shows leakage between work done and money collected
cards.use: see hours worked but less revenue billed than expected
not: measures hours billed against hours available

cards.subject: A billable rate
says: is the price charged per hour or day of a person's time
must cover cost, overhead and margin
differs from the cost rate paid for the same person
cards.use: must set what a client pays for an hour of a role
not: is what the employer pays the person per hour

cards.subject: A blended rate
says: is the average rate across a mix of roles weighted by hours
hides differences between senior and junior effort
changes if the team mix changes
cards.use: quote one rate for a team of mixed seniority
not: is the rate for a single named person

cards.subject: Project contingency
says: is an allowance added to an estimate for uncertainty in the work
is higher when scope or technology is less understood
should be explicit rather than hidden in task estimates
cards.use: estimate work with real unknowns
not: is the profit margin on the project

cards.subject: Estimate at completion
says: forecasts the total project cost once finished
can be projected from spend so far and the work completed
warns early that a project will exceed its budget
cards.use: are partway through a project and must forecast its final cost
not: is the original approved budget

cards.subject: Earned value
says: measures the budgeted value of the work actually completed
compares progress with spend to reveal cost and schedule performance
avoids reading spend as if it were progress
cards.use: want to know whether spend corresponds to real progress
not: measures only the amount invoiced to the client

cards.subject: Working capital
says: is current assets minus current liabilities
shows the short-term funds available to run the business
is tied up as receivables grow faster than payables
cards.use: need to know the cash tied up in day-to-day operations
not: is the cash raised from investors

cards.subject: Days sales outstanding
says: measures the average number of days to collect payment after a sale
is receivables divided by sales, multiplied by the days in the period
rises when customers pay slowly
cards.use: want to know how quickly customers pay
not: measures how long the company takes to pay suppliers

cards.subject: Days payable outstanding
says: measures the average number of days the company takes to pay suppliers
is payables divided by cost of sales, multiplied by the days in the period
helps cash when it is longer, within agreed terms
cards.use: want to know how long suppliers wait for payment
not: measures how long customers take to pay

cards.subject: The cash conversion cycle
says: measures the days between paying out cash and getting it back from customers
combines days sales outstanding, days inventory and days payable
is shortened by faster collection and longer supplier terms
cards.use: want to understand how long cash is tied up in operations
not: measures the days a project takes to deliver

cards.subject: A cash flow forecast
says: projects cash receipts and payments over coming weeks or months
shows when the bank balance could run short
focuses on timing rather than profit
cards.use: fear a cash shortfall before the next big payment arrives
not: projects profit over the year using accruals

cards.subject: Invoice factoring
says: sells unpaid invoices to a third party for immediate cash
brings cash forward at a cost
shortens collection time without waiting for the customer
cards.use: need cash now and have large invoices outstanding
not: extends supplier payment terms

cards.subject: A milestone billing schedule
says: splits a fee into payments tied to project stages
improves cash flow compared with billing only at the end
reduces the supplier's exposure to non-payment
cards.use: deliver a long project and want to avoid funding it all yourself
not: bills the whole fee when the project is finished

cards.subject: Overtrading
says: is growing sales faster than the cash available to fund them
can happen to a profitable company
is driven by working capital growing with sales
cards.use: see rapid growth but a shrinking bank balance
not: is trading too slowly to cover costs

cards.subject: Internal control
says: is a process that safeguards assets and keeps financial records reliable
includes approvals, reconciliations and access limits
reduces the risk of error and fraud
cards.use: want confidence that money is handled properly
not: guarantees that fraud can never occur

cards.subject: Segregation of duties
says: splits key steps of a process between different people
prevents one person from both initiating and approving a payment
reduces the risk of fraud and uncaught error
cards.use: want to stop one person controlling a payment from start to finish
not: lets one person create, approve and pay invoices

cards.subject: An audit trail
says: is a traceable record of who did what and when
lets a transaction be followed from source to ledger
supports review and investigation
cards.use: need to trace a transaction back to who approved it
not: is the final opinion of the auditor

cards.subject: Approval limits
says: set the maximum amount a role may approve alone
send larger spend to higher authority
are documented in a delegation of authority
cards.use: want larger payments to need more senior sign-off
not: stop anyone approving anything

cards.subject: A three-way match
says: compares the purchase order, goods receipt and supplier invoice before payment
catches overbilling and duplicate invoices
is a standard control in accounts payable
cards.use: want to pay only for what was ordered and received
not: compares three quotes from different suppliers

cards.subject: An external audit
says: is an independent examination of the financial statements
gives an opinion on whether they present a true and fair view
is performed by an auditor independent of management
cards.use: need an independent opinion on the accounts for investors or lenders
not: is a review run by the company's own staff

cards.subject: An internal audit
says: is a review by the organisation's own function of controls and risk
reports to management and the board on control weaknesses
can look at any process, not only financial reporting
cards.use: want an internal view of whether controls actually operate
not: is the legally required opinion on the annual accounts

cards.subject: Materiality
says: is the size of error or omission that could change a reader's decisions
guides how much audit effort a matter deserves
is judged by both size and nature
cards.use: must decide which errors are worth correcting or reporting
not: is the total value of the company's assets

cards.subject: Value added tax
says: is a consumption tax charged on sales and collected by businesses on behalf of the tax authority
is not a cost to a business that can reclaim it
is separate from income or profit tax
cards.use: invoice customers in a jurisdiction that charges a sales tax on supply
not: is a tax on company profit

cards.subject: Input VAT
says: is the tax a business pays on its purchases
may be reclaimed against tax collected on sales if the rules allow
depends on local recovery rules
cards.use: pay supplier invoices that carry sales tax
not: is the tax charged to customers on sales

cards.subject: Corporate income tax
says: is a tax charged on a company's taxable profit
is calculated under local rules that differ from accounting profit
is separate from VAT
cards.use: need to understand the tax on profit as distinct from sales taxes
not: is collected on each sale and passed to the authority

cards.subject: Withholding tax
says: is tax deducted at source from a payment to another party
is paid to the tax authority by the payer
can arise on cross-border payments depending on local rules and treaties
cards.use: pay a supplier or licensor in another country and must check deductions
not: is a tax charged only on domestic retail sales

cards.subject: Transfer pricing
says: sets the prices charged between related companies in a group
is reviewed by tax authorities for arm's-length fairness
affects where profit is reported in a group
cards.use: charge another company in the same group for services
not: sets the price charged to external customers

cards.subject: Runway
says: is the number of months the company can operate before running out of cash
is cash divided by net monthly burn
shortens as burn grows or cash falls
cards.use: want to know how long the cash will last
not: is the forecast of next year's revenue

cards.subject: Burn rate
says: is the speed at which the company spends cash
net burn subtracts incoming revenue from outgoing cash
is usually quoted per month
cards.use: want to know how fast cash is being used
not: is the total cash held at the bank

cards.subject: Equity financing
says: raises money by selling ownership shares
has no repayment schedule but dilutes existing owners
gives investors a claim on future value
cards.use: want funding without a fixed repayment obligation
not: requires repaying principal and interest on a schedule

cards.subject: Debt financing
says: raises money that must be repaid with interest
does not dilute ownership
creates fixed obligations that stay whether or not the business does well
cards.use: want funding without giving up ownership
not: gives the lender a share of ownership

cards.subject: Dilution
says: reduces existing owners' percentage when new shares are issued
does not by itself reduce the value of an owner's stake if value grows
is calculated from the new shares relative to the total
cards.use: are issuing shares to a new investor
not: happens when the company repays a loan

cards.subject: A cap table
says: lists who owns how much of the company and in what form
is updated by each financing round
shows the effect of new shares on every holder
cards.use: need to see how ownership is split among founders and investors
not: lists the company's customers

cards.subject: Pre-money valuation
says: is the value of the company before new investment is added
plus the new money gives the post-money valuation
sets the price per share for the round
cards.use: negotiate the value placed on the company before the investor's cash arrives
not: includes the new investment

cards.subject: Post-money valuation
says: is the pre-money valuation plus the new investment
determines the investor's percentage as their money divided by the post-money figure
is the figure used to compute dilution in the round
cards.use: need to work out the percentage a new investor will own
not: is the value before the investment

cards.subject: A convertible note
says: is a loan that converts into shares at a later financing
defers setting a valuation
often carries a discount or cap on the conversion price
cards.use: want to raise quickly without agreeing a valuation yet
not: is repaid in cash with no conversion

cards.subject: A term sheet
says: summarises the main terms of an investment before final contracts
is generally non-binding on the main terms
sets items such as valuation, investment size and investor rights
cards.use: have an investor interested and want terms agreed before lawyers draft contracts
not: is the final signed shareholders' agreement

cards.subject: Management accounts
says: are internal financial reports prepared monthly for decision making
are not the audited statutory accounts
give leaders timely profit, cash and balance sheet figures
cards.use: need timely numbers between annual audits
not: are the audited annual accounts filed publicly

cards.subject: A board pack
says: is the set of papers sent to directors before a board meeting
includes financial results, budget comparison, cash and key metrics
should lead with the decisions and exceptions that need attention
cards.use: must report finances to directors before a meeting
not: is the audited annual accounts

cards.subject: Budget-versus-actual reporting
says: compares planned figures with real results for the period
explains the main variances with commentary
shows directors where performance departs from plan
cards.use: want the board to see how results compare with plan
not: compares this year's results with a competitor's

cards.subject: A debt covenant
says: is a condition in a loan agreement that the borrower must keep to
may set limits on ratios such as debt to earnings
can allow the lender to act if broken
cards.use: hold a loan that sets financial conditions on the business
not: is the interest rate of the loan

qa.q: A company has revenue of 200,000 and direct delivery costs of 80,000. What is its gross margin percentage?
qa.right: 60 percent
qa.why: Gross profit is 200,000 minus 80,000, which is 120,000, and 120,000 divided by 200,000 is 60 percent.

qa.q: Monthly recurring revenue is 25,000. What is the annual recurring revenue?
qa.why: ARR is MRR multiplied by twelve.

qa.q: A company holds 1,200,000 in cash and its net burn is 100,000 a month. What is its runway?
qa.right: 12 months
qa.why: Runway is cash divided by net monthly burn.

qa.q: A project costs 120,000 and saves 5,000 a month. What is the simple payback period?
qa.right: 24 months
qa.why: 120,000 divided by 5,000 is 24 months.

qa.q: A product sells for 100 and has a variable cost of 40. What is the contribution margin per unit?
qa.why: Contribution per unit is price minus variable cost.

qa.q: A company loses 10 of its 200 customers in a month. What is the monthly logo churn rate?
qa.right: 5 percent
qa.why: 10 divided by 200 is 5 percent.

qa.q: A consultant works 30 billable hours in a 40-hour week. What is the utilisation rate?
qa.right: 75 percent
qa.why: Billable hours divided by available hours is 30 divided by 40.

qa.q: An item costs 80 to make and is sold with a 25 percent markup on cost. What is the selling price?
qa.why: A 25 percent markup on 80 adds 20.

qa.q: A sale with a 25 percent markup on cost has what margin on selling price?
qa.right: 20 percent
qa.why: Cost 80, price 100: profit 20 is 20 percent of the price.

qa.q: A budget line was 50,000 and the actual spend was 56,000. How is the variance described?
qa.right: 6,000 unfavourable, 12 percent over budget
qa.why: Spending above budget reduces profit, so it is unfavourable; 6,000 divided by 50,000 is 12 percent.

qa.q: A customer pays 1,200 for a twelve-month subscription on 1 January. How much revenue is recognised by the end of March?
qa.why: Revenue is recognised across the service period: three months at 100 each.

qa.q: An equipment purchase of 30,000 has a five-year useful life and no residual value. What is the annual straight-line depreciation?
qa.why: 30,000 divided by 5 years is 6,000.

qa.q: Capitalised software costing 240,000 is amortised over four years. What is the yearly charge?
qa.why: 240,000 divided by 4 is 60,000.

qa.q: A supplier contract rises by 5 percent a year. The first year costs 100,000. What does the second year cost?
qa.why: 5 percent of 100,000 is 5,000.

qa.q: Which cost is a variable cost for an online service?
qa.right: Payment processing fee per transaction
qa.why: It rises with each transaction.

qa.q: Why can a profitable company run out of cash?
qa.right: Profit is recorded on accruals, so customers may not yet have paid
wrong: Profit and cash are always identical
qa.why: Profit counts earned revenue, cash counts money received.

qa.q: A customer pays 100 a month, gross margin is 60 percent and the acquisition cost is 1,200. What is the CAC payback?
qa.right: 20 months
qa.why: Monthly gross profit is 60, and 1,200 divided by 60 is 20 months.

qa.q: A customer pays 100 a month at an 80 percent gross margin with 4 percent monthly churn. What is the approximate LTV?
qa.why: LTV is 100 multiplied by 0.8 divided by 0.04.

qa.q: A product sells for 50 with variable cost of 20 per unit and fixed costs of 6,000. How many units are needed to break even?
qa.why: Contribution per unit is 30, and 6,000 divided by 30 is 200.

qa.q: A fixed-price project is quoted at 90,000 with an estimated cost of 63,000. What is the expected project margin?
qa.right: 30 percent
qa.why: Profit 27,000 divided by 90,000 is 30 percent.

qa.q: Receivables are 60,000 and annual sales are 730,000. Using a 365-day year, what are the days sales outstanding?
qa.right: 30 days
qa.why: 60,000 divided by 730,000 multiplied by 365 is 30.

qa.q: A cloud bill of 50,000 served 25 million requests. What is the cost per 1,000 requests?
qa.why: 50,000 divided by 25,000 thousand-request units is 2.

qa.q: A salary of 80,000 carries on-costs of 25 percent of salary, plus 5,000 of equipment. What is the fully loaded annual cost?
qa.why: 80,000 plus 20,000 on-costs plus 5,000 equipment.

qa.q: A company raises 2 million at an 8 million pre-money valuation. What share do the new investors own?
qa.right: 20 percent
qa.why: Post-money is 10 million, and 2 divided by 10 is 20 percent.

qa.q: Revenue is 150,000 a month and cash spending is 400,000. With 1.5 million in cash, what is the runway?
qa.right: 6 months
qa.why: Net burn is 250,000 and 1,500,000 divided by 250,000 is 6.

qa.q: A team has 2 seniors billed at 150 an hour and 3 juniors billed at 100 an hour. What is the blended rate?
qa.why: (2 times 150 plus 3 times 100) divided by 5 is 600 divided by 5.

qa.q: Customers pay in 45 days on average and the company pays suppliers in 30 days, with no inventory. What is the cash conversion cycle?
qa.right: 15 days
qa.why: 45 minus 30 gives 15 days of cash tied up.

qa.q: A project has a budget of 100,000. 60,000 is spent and the work is 50 percent complete. At the same efficiency, what is the estimate at completion?
qa.why: 60,000 spent for half the work implies 120,000 in total.

qa.q: An investment of 100 returns 110 in exactly one year. At a 10 percent discount rate, what is its net present value?
qa.right: Zero
qa.why: 110 divided by 1.1 is 100, which equals the outlay.

qa.q: Net benefit is 70,000 against an investment cost of 50,000. What is the ROI?
qa.right: 40 percent
qa.why: Gain of 20,000 over cost of 50,000 is 40 percent.

qa.q: Starting recurring revenue is 1,000, with 150 expansion, 50 contraction and 100 churn. What is net revenue retention?
qa.right: 100 percent
qa.why: 1,000 plus 150 minus 50 minus 100 is 1,000.

qa.q: With the same figures as 1,000 start, 150 expansion, 50 contraction and 100 churn, what is gross revenue retention?
qa.right: 85 percent
qa.why: Only churn and contraction count: 1,000 minus 150 divided by 1,000.

qa.q: On-demand usage costs 10,000 a month. A commitment gives 30 percent off for the committed amount. What is the monthly cost if all of it is committed and used?
qa.why: 30 percent off 10,000 leaves 7,000.

qa.q: A project has a budget of 100,000 and you earned 40 percent of the planned value while spending 55,000. What does this indicate?
qa.right: Cost is running ahead of progress
wrong: Nothing, because spending is below budget
qa.why: Spending 55,000 for work worth 40,000 means more cost than progress.

qa.q: Which measure includes one-off setup fees?
qa.right: Total revenue
qa.why: Recurring metrics exclude one-off fees; total revenue does not.

qa.q: Why is a gross margin figure for a software company reduced by hosting and support costs?
qa.right: They are direct costs of delivering the service
qa.why: Cost of revenue includes the direct cost of delivering the service.

qa.q: Which cost is normally expensed rather than capitalised?
qa.right: Routine maintenance and bug fixing on a live product
wrong: Building a new, viable product that will be used for years
Purchasing servers for own data centre
qa.why: Maintenance generally keeps the asset working rather than creating a new one.

qa.q: A company's net revenue retention is 120 percent but its gross revenue retention is 70 percent. What does this suggest?
qa.right: A small number of expanding accounts are masking a leaky base
wrong: The base is healthy because both numbers are high
New customers are driving the figure
qa.why: Large expansion hides heavy churn and contraction.

qa.q: The cloud bill grew 40 percent but traffic was flat. What should you check first?
qa.right: Which teams or resources the new spend belongs to, using tags and cost reports
wrong: Whether to cut every team's budget by 40 percent
Whether to buy a three-year commitment immediately
qa.why: Attribution shows where the growth is before any remedy is chosen.

qa.q: Sales offers a 10 percent discount for paying a year up front. Finance asks how the cash will be reported. What is correct?
qa.right: Cash is received at once but revenue is recognised over the year, with the rest held as deferred revenue
wrong: All the revenue is recognised on the day of payment
No revenue is recognised until the year ends
The cash is recorded as profit when it arrives
qa.why: Revenue follows delivery, so prepaid amounts begin as a liability.

qa.q: A key supplier contract auto-renews unless notice is given in 60 days, and nobody owns the date. What should you do first?
qa.right: Record the notice deadline, assign an owner and decide whether to renegotiate or exit
wrong: Wait for the supplier to remind you
Assume you can cancel after the renewal
Let it renew and review it next year
qa.why: The notice window is what preserves your options.

qa.q: An engineering lead wants to capitalise the salaries of all engineers, including those fixing bugs on a live product. What is the best response?
qa.right: Capitalise only effort that creates a qualifying new asset and expense maintenance, following the accounting policy
wrong: Approve it because salaries are always capital
qa.why: Capitalisation depends on the nature of the work, not on who does it.

qa.q: A fixed-price project is 80 percent through its budget but only 50 percent complete. What should the delivery manager do?
qa.right: Re-estimate the cost to complete, raise it with the sponsor now and address scope or change control
wrong: Wait until the budget is exhausted
Hide the overrun to keep the margin
Ask the team to work unrecorded hours
qa.why: Early re-forecasting preserves options and trust.

qa.q: A growing agency shows a profit every month but its bank balance keeps falling. What is the most likely cause?
qa.right: Receivables and work in progress are growing faster than cash is collected
wrong: Depreciation is paid in cash each month
Profit is overstated by exactly the bank fees
qa.why: Working capital absorbs cash even while accruals show profit.

qa.q: A SaaS company has strong new-customer growth but net revenue retention of 85 percent. What is the concern?
qa.right: The existing base shrinks each year, so acquisition spend is partly refilling a leaking bucket
wrong: Growth is healthy because new customers are increasing
It is a sign of too much expansion revenue
qa.why: Net retention below 100 percent means the base loses revenue on its own.

qa.q: An employee can create a supplier, approve its invoice and release payment. Which control is missing?
qa.right: Segregation of duties
qa.why: One person controlling the whole chain creates fraud risk.

qa.q: A utilisation target of 95 percent is proposed for a delivery team. What is the main risk?
qa.right: No time for training, sales support or absorbing variation, leading to burnout and weaker quality
wrong: Margins will fall because hours are too few
Billable rates will have to be reduced
qa.why: Very high utilisation leaves no slack.

qa.q: A vendor offers a big discount for a three-year minimum commitment, but the product roadmap is uncertain. What is the best approach?
qa.right: Weigh the saving against the exit risk, test volume scenarios and seek flexibility such as termination rights or a lower commitment
wrong: Sign and plan to reduce use later
qa.why: A discount is only valuable if the commitment will actually be used.

qa.q: A founder wants to start fundraising when cash will last four months. What is the main problem?
qa.right: A raise often takes months, so short runway weakens negotiating position
wrong: Investors prefer companies with less cash
Fundraising can be completed in days
Runway has no effect on valuation
qa.why: Needing money quickly reduces leverage.

qa.q: The LTV calculation uses revenue per customer instead of gross profit. What is the effect?
qa.right: It overstates the value of a customer
qa.why: Revenue ignores the cost of serving the customer.

qa.q: A usage-based product has seen its hosting costs spike. Which pricing check is most useful?
qa.right: Whether price per unit still covers cost per unit with margin
wrong: Whether the contract term is long enough
Whether the discount rate has changed
qa.why: Unit price must exceed unit cost for usage-based growth to be profitable.

qa.q: Budget owners habitually spend everything left in November. Which change best addresses this?
qa.right: Review budgets by outcomes and allow justified carry-over or rolling forecasts
wrong: Cut all budgets by a fixed percentage
Announce that overspend will be ignored
qa.why: The behaviour is created by use-it-or-lose-it rules.

qa.q: Forecasts keep missing because the team extrapolates last year. Which approach is most helpful?
qa.right: Build a driver-based forecast using hiring, customer and usage assumptions
wrong: Add a fixed 10 percent to last year
qa.why: Drivers connect the numbers to the business.

qa.q: A team asks to buy a long-term cloud commitment for a service it has not yet rightsized. What should you advise?
qa.right: Rightsize first and then commit to the confirmed baseline
wrong: Commit now to a bigger size to be safe
Commit to double the current use
qa.why: Committing to waste locks the waste in.

qa.q: A project has a positive NPV but the board prefers one with a faster payback. Which statement is most accurate?
qa.right: NPV measures total value created and payback measures speed of recovery, so they answer different questions
wrong: Payback is always better than NPV
The two measures always rank projects identically
qa.why: Each metric has a purpose and a blind spot.

qa.q: A supplier's SLA credit is capped at a fraction of the monthly fee, yet an outage costs the business far more. What does this show?
qa.right: Service credits compensate poorly for real loss, so resilience planning cannot rely on them
wrong: The supplier is in breach of law
qa.why: The remedy is limited by design.

qa.q: A board pack contains forty pages of detailed ledgers. What is the best improvement?
qa.right: Lead with a short summary of results, variances, risks and decisions needed, with detail in appendices
wrong: Send it the evening before the meeting
qa.why: Board reporting should direct attention to decisions.

qa.q: Two options have the same build cost. One needs far more support and licences. What should the comparison use?
qa.right: Total cost of ownership over the expected life
qa.why: Run cost often dominates over a long life.

qa.q: A company cancels a product after capitalising its development cost. What accounting consequence normally follows?
qa.right: An impairment charge for the unrecoverable capitalised amount
wrong: The cost moves to deferred revenue
qa.why: Assets that will not generate benefit are written down.

qa.q: A manager treats a markup of 30 percent as a 30 percent margin when quoting. What is the result?
qa.right: Margin is actually lower than 30 percent, about 23 percent
qa.why: A 30 percent markup on cost 100 gives price 130 and margin 30/130, about 23 percent.
